intro: The story of the Watchers did not stop with 1 Enoch. Centuries later, New Testament writers still remembered it. Jude quotes 1 Enoch by name. Second Peter speaks of angels put in Tartarus. First Peter tells of spirits in prison from Noah's day. Paul writes again and again about rulers, authorities and powers. This unit reads those passages closely, in translation, with attention to the Greek words behind them.

Michael Heiser argued that these writers read Genesis 6 and Deuteronomy 32 the way many Jews of their time did, through books like 1 Enoch. For him, the powers in Paul's letters are the rebel gods of the nations. Other scholars read the same verses in other ways: as human rulers, as structures of society, or as a rebellion before Eden. You will meet each reading and the evidence behind it.

By the end of the unit, you will be able to compare Jude 14–15 with 1 Enoch 1:9. You will explain three readings of 1 Peter 3:19 and several readings of Paul's powers. You will also explain why Jude's quotation did not bring 1 Enoch into most Bibles, but did not stop one ancient church from keeping it.
bigQuestion: How did New Testament writers remember the Watchers and the gods of the nations, and how have readers understood what they wrote?

timeline.t: Hesiod's Theogony describes Tartarus, the prison of the Titans
The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36) is written, most scholars think
Aramaic copies of 1 Enoch are made; some are later found at Qumran
Paul writes letters including Galatians, 1 Corinthians and Romans
Jude, 1 Peter and 2 Peter are written (exact dates are debated)
Tertullian argues that the Book of Enoch should be respected
Eusebius lists Jude among the disputed books
Jerome writes that many reject Jude because it quotes Enoch
James Bruce brings Ge'ez copies of 1 Enoch from Ethiopia to Europe
R. H. Charles publishes his English translation, The Book of Enoch
The Dead Sea Scrolls are found near Qumran, with Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch
Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm (2015) and Reversing Hermon (2017)

test.q: Which passage in 1 Enoch does Jude 14–15 quote?
test.why: Jude 14–15 closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, the prophecy of the Lord coming with his holy ones.

test.q: In Genesis 5, why is Enoch 'the seventh from Adam'?
choices: He is the seventh name in the line, counting Adam
He was born on the seventh day
test.why: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared and Enoch make seven names.

test.q: Which verse describes angels who kept not their first estate?
test.why: Jude 6 speaks of angels who left their proper home and are kept in chains.

test.q: In Greek stories, who was imprisoned in Tartarus?
test.why: Hesiod's Theogony tells of the Titans held in Tartarus.

test.q: Which order of judgments does 2 Peter 2:4–8 follow?
test.why: Second Peter keeps the Genesis order: the angels, Noah's flood, then Sodom.

test.q: In Heiser's reading of 1 Peter 3:19, what did Christ proclaim to the spirits in prison?
test.why: Heiser read the proclamation as an announcement of victory to the imprisoned Watchers.

test.q: Which early bishop read 1 Peter 3:19 as Christ preaching through Noah?
test.why: Augustine held that Christ's Spirit spoke through Noah to the people of his day.

test.q: Why did Jerome say many people rejected Jude?
choices: It quoted the Book of Enoch
test.why: Jerome wrote in 393 CE that Jude's quotation of Enoch made many reject it.

test.q: Which churches keep 1 Enoch in their Bibles?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
The Greek and Russian Orthodox churches
test.why: Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo and Eritrean Orthodox churches include 1 Enoch in their canon.

test.q: What does the Dead Sea Scrolls text of Deuteronomy 32:8 read, instead of 'sons of Israel'?
test.why: A Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript reads 'sons of God'; the Septuagint has 'angels of God'.

test.q: According to Heiser, who are the rulers and authorities in Paul's letters?
choices: The rebel gods of the nations from Deuteronomy 32
test.why: Heiser tied Paul's powers to the sons of God placed over the nations.

test.q: In 1 Corinthians 10:20, Paul says the nations sacrifice to what?
test.why: Paul echoes Deuteronomy 32:17: the sacrifices go to daimonia, not to God.

test.q: Which is one reading of the stoicheia in Galatians 4:3, 9?
choices: Spiritual beings linked with the elements or stars
test.why: Readers take stoicheia as basic principles, physical elements or spiritual beings.

test.q: What image does Colossians 2:15 use for the defeat of the powers?
choices: A Roman triumph, a victory parade
test.why: The verb thriambeuō pictures leading defeated enemies in a triumph.

test.q: How did Walter Wink read Paul's powers?
choices: As the inner spirit of institutions
As the letters of the alphabet
test.why: Wink, starting in 1984, read the powers as the inner spirit of institutions such as nations and companies.

write.prompt: Who are the 'spirits in prison' in 1 Peter 3:19? Cite 1 Peter 3:18–22 and at least two of these: Jude 6, 2 Peter 2:4–5, 1 Enoch 12–16. Explain what each text says, then compare Heiser's reading with one other reading from this unit.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse each time you cite a text.
Attribute every reading: 'Heiser argues…', 'Augustine read…', 'other scholars think…'.
Compare the readings fairly; you do not need to pick a winner.
Use the unit's terms, such as tartaroō, kēryssō and Watchers, and explain each one.
